docs.title: oboromi
docs.text:
oboromi is a work-in-progress Nintendo Switch 2 emulator written in Rust. These pages explain how it is built, with most of the depth in the GPU work: translating the Switch 2's Ampere shader code to Vulkan and driving it from guest pushbuffers.

start here for Architecture map one diagram of the whole emulator and a line per page Decision records why the GPU work is shaped the way it is Glossary the terms the pages use SM86 instruction table (PDF) every SM86 encoding class, generated from the instruction table

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Each term is explained once, here. The architecture pages use them without repeating the explanation.

flowchart LR
    GPFIFO --> PB["pushbuffer"] --> M["methods"]
    M --> C3["3D class: SPH, cbuf, TIC/TSC"]
    M --> CC["compute class: QMD"]
    C3 --> SASS
    CC --> SASS
    SASS -->|"translator"| SPIRV["SPIR-V"]
term meaning SASS NVIDIA's native GPU machine code. On SM86 every instruction is 128 bits, with its scheduling bits inside the word. SM86 the Ampere instruction set of the GA102 family (RTX 3090, A6000). The Switch 2's T239 uses the same encoding table. T239 the Switch 2's system-on-chip. Its GPU is the GA10F, an Ampere part. GA102 the desktop Ampere chip the silicon captures come from. SPIR-V the binary shader language Vulkan consumes. The translator writes it. spirv-val the Khronos validator for SPIR-V modules. nvdisasm NVIDIA's disassembler. It carries the instruction table the decoder is generated from. lavapipe Mesa's Vulkan driver that runs on the CPU (also called llvmpipe). The CI device. GPFIFO the ring of 8-byte entries a channel reads. Each entry points at a pushbuffer and gives its length. pushbuffer a list of 32-bit words in guest memory: method headers followed by their data. method a register write to a GPU class, addressed by offset. subchannel one of eight slots a channel binds a class to with SET_OBJECT; each method header names one. class a GPU engine's register interface: 0xC797 is the Ampere 3D class, 0xC7C0 compute, 0xC76F the channel. MME the macro engine that expands macro calls into method writes. Ampere uses MME64. QMD queue meta data: the 256-byte compute launch descriptor in guest memory (grid, block, program, cbufs). SPH shader program header: the block before a graphics program that names its stage and the attributes it reads and writes. IMAP, OMAP the SPH's input and output attribute maps. cbuf constant buffer: a read-only buffer a shader reads with c[bank][offset]. Bank 0 carries launch data for compute. TIC texture image control: a 32-byte texture header in a pool (format, size, layout, address, mips). TSC texture sampler control: a 32-byte sampler entry in a pool (wrap, filters, LOD). handle a cbuf word whose low 20 bits index the TIC pool and top 12 bits the TSC pool. block-linear NVIDIA's tiled texture layout made of GOBs; pitch-linear is plain rows. GOB group of bytes: 64 bytes by 8 rows, the tile block-linear is built from. warp 32 threads that run one instruction stream together; a lane is one of them. BSSY, BSYNC the SM86 pair that marks where diverged lanes of a warp reconverge. HMMA, IMMA warp-wide matrix multiply-accumulate on tensor cores, for floats and integers. uniform datapath the per-warp scalar registers UR0 to UR62 and predicates UP0 to UP6. VA, PA GPU virtual address and guest-physical address. cubin an ELF file holding compiled CUDA kernels for one SM version. HLE high-level emulation: implementing a firmware service's behaviour instead of running its code. Unicorn the CPU emulator library oboromi's ARM cores run on.

Sources: core/src/gpu/{fifo,threed,texture,engine}.rs, core/src/gpu/compute_class.rs on gpu/qmd-dispatch, NVIDIA's open-gpu-doc class headers.

docs.title: Decision records
docs.text:
One page per decision that shaped the GPU work, in the MADR shape: the problem, the choice, what it costs, and how we know it holds. Each record names its component in the front matter.

ADR decision 0001 every resource lives in descriptor set 0 at fixed or dense bindings 0002 guest global memory is one storage buffer window 0003 divergent programs run workgroup-uniform with tracked reconvergence 0004 guest memory is the authority; host copies follow page generations 0005 tensor sums use the silicon model, emitted as DontUnroll loops 0006 the pusher runs synchronously and hands out draw snapshots 0007 the T239 decodes with the SM86 instruction table 0008 silicon captures are the reference, known failures are per device

docs.title: One descriptor set with fixed and dense bindings
Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: A translated program reads host support data, up to eight guest cbufs, global memory, and any number of textures and surfaces. Compute and graphics pipelines must agree on where each one lives, and graphics has two stages sharing one layout.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Everything lives in set 0. Binding 0 is a host support uniform buffer, never a guest cbuf. Bindings 1 to 8 are guest cbuf slots 0 to 7 as std140 uvec4 arrays. Binding 9 is the global memory window, 10 and 11 the test-only register in and out buffers. Textures and surfaces take dense bindings from 12 in first-use order, deduplicated by where their handle comes from. Only used bindings are emitted.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because one Descriptors type serves compute and graphics, and a module's resource list is all the host needs to bind it.
  • Good, because support data can never collide with what the guest put in cbuf 0.
  • Bad, because two stages that read the same cbuf slot from different buffers cannot share a pipeline; the engine rejects that by name.
  • Bad, because dynamic texture indexing will need descriptor arrays beside this layout.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
spirv-val on every module, the Vulkan validation layer on dispatch and draw, and the texture tests that bind several images at once.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/mod.rs, core/src/gpu/compute.rs.

docs.title: One storage buffer window for guest global memory
Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: SASS loads and stores use 64-bit guest addresses. Vulkan shaders cannot dereference guest addresses, and buffer device addresses are host pointers that know nothing of the guest's page tables.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: All global memory a dispatch touches is one storage buffer at binding 9. The host resolves the guest range through the page map, gathers it into one buffer aligned down to 16 bytes, and puts the window's base VA in the support buffer. A translated LDG or STG subtracts the base and indexes the buffer. Unmapped ranges fail; buffer device addresses are not used.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because one rule covers every load, store and atomic, at any width up to 128 bits.
  • Good, because a missing mapping is an error, not a wild access.
  • Bad, because the window must hold every byte the program may touch, so scattered accesses copy more than they use.
  • Bad, because LDG and STG with a memory descriptor need care: the descriptor is not part of the address.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The compiled mul-add kernel and the gradient program match silicon through this window, and the memory tests cover remaps.

Sources: core/src/gpu/memory.rs window, core/src/gpu/sm86/access.rs, core/src/tests/gpu/harness.rs run_grid.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The translator runs each lane as a loop over a guest pc. Warp collectives (VOTE, SHFL, MATCH, REDUX, tensor ops) and BAR trade data through workgroup barriers, which every invocation must reach together. With lanes at different pcs that is undefined behaviour, and partial-mask votes could not be replayed.

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• Structurize the guest control flow into Vulkan loops and selections.
  • Native subgroup operations only.
  • Keep the pc loop and schedule it uniformly across the workgroup.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Keep the pc loop. A program with collectives or BAR steps every invocation together: each step the workgroup votes the lowest runnable pc, lanes at that pc run it, the rest sit out with memory effects masked. BSSY and BSYNC tokens are tracked per lane, and BAR arrivals per barrier id until the required lanes arrive. Programs without collectives keep the free per-lane loop. Shared-memory exchange is the reference everywhere.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because divergent votes, shuffles and barriers match silicon, including the partial-mask cases.
  • Good, because it runs on lavapipe, whose subgroups are 8 lanes wide.
  • Bad, because programs with collectives pay a vote and a barrier per step.
  • Bad, because fairness under spin loops is not verified.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The warp scoreboard passes on Intel and lavapipe, and tests cover unequal branch lengths, nested tokens and early exit.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/mod.rs translate_program, core/src/gpu/sm86/warp.rs.

docs.title: Guest memory is the authority for coherence
Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The engine keeps host copies of guest data: buffer mirrors, render targets, compiled modules. The guest can remap a VA, write a buffer from the CPU, or render into memory it later samples. Host copies must never show what guest memory does not hold.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Guest RAM is the one source of truth. Every host resource is keyed by the guest-physical ranges behind it, not by VA. A MemoryTracker stamps each physical page write with a global generation and its writer. A mirror refreshes when its ranges' generation moved. Every draw writes its target back to guest RAM before submit returns, and stores the generation it left. A target whose pages changed outside its own draws is an error until loading it is implemented.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because remaps and aliasing are correct by construction, and render to texture is a read of guest memory.
  • Good, because a CPU read after submit always sees GPU results.
  • Bad, because every draw pays a readback; fine for the demos, not for a title at full speed.
  • Bad, because page granularity refreshes whole pages for small writes.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The engine acceptance test remaps a vertex VA between draws and checks the next draw follows it.

Sources: core/src/gpu/memory.rs, core/src/gpu/engine.rs.

docs.title: Exact HMMA accumulation as DontUnroll loops
Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: Silicon sums HMMA products in groups, aligned to the largest exponent and truncated, not in IEEE order. An IEEE fma chain disagreed with the tensor captures. Written out in full, the exact model made each HMMA a module drivers were slow to compile; as one SPIR-V function, both drivers inlined it back.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Implement the silicon model exactly: groups of eight k (four for TF32), alignment to the largest exponent, truncation below it, an exact integer sum, truncating normalisation, per-group rounding for .F16, and IEEE handling of only the inf and NaN terms. Stage the operands once in a Private array and run the sum in four DontUnroll loops with Private scalars instead of phis.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because the tensor scoreboard is bit-exact on Intel and lavapipe.
  • Good, because cold compile is fast again on both drivers.
  • Bad, because Intel spills registers in this form, and warm runs are slightly slower than the IEEE form.
  • Bad, because the loops rely on drivers honouring DontUnroll, checked on Intel and lavapipe only.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The tensor silicon scoreboard and the per-op compile timings in textures and tensors.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/tensor.rs, core/src/tests/gpu/tensor.rs.

docs.title: A synchronous pusher that hands out draw snapshots
Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: A pushbuffer interleaves state writes, draws, cbuf updates, clears and semaphore releases. The order they take effect in matters, and a host GPU queue runs on its own clock. There is no guest OS layer yet to wait on fences or syncpoints.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Pusher::submit decodes GPFIFO entries to completion and returns an ordered list of events. The 3D class keeps raw register words and copies the state a draw needs into an immutable DrawSnapshot at the draw trigger. LOAD_CONSTANT_BUFFER, reports and semaphore releases are events in the same list, so they apply in pushbuffer order. The engine runs each event before the next, and Gpu::submit returns when every draw is back in guest memory. No MME, no queue overlap.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because ordering is trivially right, and tests read results right after submit.
  • Good, because the pusher and the 3D class are plain data code, tested without a device.
  • Bad, because the CPU waits for the GPU on every submit; real titles will need guest fences decoupled from host fences.
  • Bad, because macro-driven pushbuffers fail until MME64 exists.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
core/src/tests/gpu/fifo.rs for decode and ordering, and the engine acceptance test for the report and the semaphore payloads landing in guest memory.

Sources: core/src/gpu/fifo.rs, core/src/gpu/threed.rs, core/src/gpu/engine.rs.

docs.title: The T239 decodes with the SM86 instruction table
Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The decoder is generated from the SM86 instruction table. The Switch 2's T239 has a GA10F GPU, which CUDA calls SM88. If its encodings differ, every handler keyed on SM86 is wrong in places.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Keep the SM86 table. CUDA 13.1's nvdisasm accepts --binary SM88, and its embedded tables for SM86, SM87 and SM88 are byte-identical. Against the committed table: no class added or removed, no bit field changed, no encoding key changed. The only differences are opcode names that became internal, which would break the generated handler names. Every fixture word disassembles the same under SM86 and SM88. open-gpu-doc also lists the T239 under the same 3D class as the GA102 family.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because silicon captures from a desktop GA102 check the same encodings the T239 runs.
  • Good, because the public opcode names stay readable.
  • Bad, because execution semantics are verified on GA102, not on a T239; equality there is assumed, by design.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The extracted SM88 table is kept on gpu/sm88-table beside a diff summary; regenerate and diff when a new CUDA ships.

Sources: scripts/sm_86_instructions.txt, scripts/decoder_generator.rs, CUDA 13.1 nvdisasm, open-gpu-doc classes/3d.

docs.title: Silicon is the reference; known failures are per device
Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: There is no trustworthy public SM86 assembler and no complete semantic reference. Hand-built encodings have been wrong before, and documentation and other emulators cover Maxwell, not Ampere. Vulkan drivers also differ in float rounding, denormals and NaNs.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Results are checked against registers read back from real Ampere cards. A capture patches one instruction word into an nvcc-built seed kernel, runs it through the CUDA driver API, and records inputs and outputs; observed results are never hand-written. Encodings are checked with nvdisasm first. The scoreboard tests replay every capture on each device and fail on any mismatch not listed. Allowed mismatches are listed by fixture id with a reason, either for every device or for lavapipe only.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because bugs no reading of documentation would find were found: NaN rules, tensor rounding, shuffle clamping.
  • Good, because a device quirk cannot hide a translator bug: it is excused for that device only.
  • Bad, because each session costs a rented card and some seeds fault, so coverage arrives in batches.
  • Bad, because the captures come from GA102, not from a Switch 2.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
fixtures_match_silicon, fixtures_match_warp_silicon and fixtures_match_tensor_silicon pass on Intel and lavapipe.

Sources: core/tests/fixtures/README, core/src/tests/gpu/fixtures.rs.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
oboromi emulates the Nintendo Switch 2. The CPU side runs ARM code on Unicorn over one flat RAM block, the firmware services are named stubs, and nothing loads a game yet. The GPU side is the part with real depth: it reads guest pushbuffers, translates the guest's SM86 shader machine code (SASS) to SPIR-V and runs it on any Vulkan device.

flowchart TB
    GUI["Qt GUI<br/>gui-qt"] -->|"C FFI"| FFI["ffi.rs"]
    FFI --> SYS["sys::State<br/>services"]
    FFI --> CPU["cpu<br/>8 Unicorn cores"]
    CPU --- RAM[("guest RAM<br/>one flat block")]
    SYS --> NN["nn<br/>service stubs"]
    FFI --> ENG
    subgraph GPU["gpu"]
        FIFO["fifo + threed<br/>command processor"] --> ENG["engine<br/>draws over guest memory"]
        ENG --> SASS["sm86<br/>SASS to SPIR-V"]
        ENG --> VK["compute + graphics<br/>Vulkan backend"]
        SASS --> VK
        CUDA["cubin<br/>CUDA kernel loader"] --> SASS
    end
    ENG --> DISP["display.rs<br/>last frame"]
    DISP -->|"frame callback"| GUI
    classDef gpu stroke:#61b7df,stroke-width:3px
    class FIFO,ENG,SASS,VK,CUDA gpu

The blue-outlined boxes are the GPU work these pages describe. Everything else is context.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: The choices that shaped the GPU work are recorded as ADRs under docs/adr: one page each, with the problem, the decision and what it costs.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
New to the code: overview, then GPU pipeline, then the subsystem you are touching. Reviewing a GPU PR: GPU pipeline for the branch map, then verification for what has to pass.

Verified by: every page names its own checks in a "Verified by" line.

Sources: core/src/lib.rs, core/src/gpu/mod.rs, gui-qt/src/MainWindow.cpp, README.md.

docs.title: Command processor and memory
docs.text: The command processor reads GPFIFO entries, splits pushbuffers into method writes and routes each write to the class bound on its subchannel. Guest memory sits behind a GPU page map, and the guest's own RAM stays the one copy every host resource is checked against.

docs.title: GPFIFO and method headers
docs.text:
item bits meaning entry word 0 31:2 pushbuffer address, low part entry word 1 7:0, 9, 30:10, 31 address high byte, level, length in words, sync header 11:0 method, as a word index header 15:13 subchannel header 28:16 count, or the value for immediate mode header 31:29 mode: 1 incrementing, 3 non-incrementing, 4 immediate, 5 increment once, 7 end of segment

Methods below 0x40 belong to the channel: SET_OBJECT binds a class id to the subchannel, SEMAPHORE_A to D produce acquire and release events. Anything else goes to the bound class, and an unbound subchannel or unknown class is an error.

flowchart LR
    GP["GPFIFO entry"] --> PB["pushbuffer words"]
    PB --> HDR{"method < 0x40?"}
    HDR -->|"yes"| CH["channel<br/>SET_OBJECT, semaphores"]
    HDR -->|"no"| SUB{"class on subchannel"}
    SUB -->|"0xC797"| TD["3D register file<br/>DrawSnapshot"]
    SUB -->|"0xC7C0"| CC["compute class, own branch<br/>QMD, DispatchSnapshot"]
    SUB -->|"other"| ERR["error by name"]

docs.title: The 3D class, 0xC797
docs.text: ThreeD keeps the raw register words plus dirty groups (vertex streams, attributes, colour targets, viewport and scissor, shader programs, cbuf binds, blend and depth, index buffer). At a draw trigger it emits a DrawSnapshot: topology, counts, vertex streams and attributes, the six shader program slots, colour target 0, viewport, scissor, write mask, depth, cull, blend flags, the index buffer and the bound cbufs per binding group. LOAD_CONSTANT_BUFFER is an ordered event too, so cbuf updates between draws land in order.

docs.title: The compute class, 0xC7C0
docs.text: On gpu/qmd-dispatch: writing SEND_SIGNALING_PCAS_B fetches the 256-byte QMD at SEND_PCAS_A and decodes QMDV02_03 into a DispatchSnapshot: program address, grid, block, shared size, eight cbufs, two release semaphores, barrier and register counts, shared and local windows, sampler and texture pools. Other QMD versions are rejected.

docs.title: Page map and coherence
docs.text:
PageMap maps GPU VA pages to guest-physical pages, one map per address space, in 64 KiB pages (the big page size Ryujinx maps with; the T239 value is unverified). Unmapped ranges are errors, never a guess. MemoryTracker stamps every write to a physical page with a global generation and its writer, CPU or GPU.

resource keyed by refreshed when buffer mirror (vertices, cbufs) guest-physical ranges the ranges' generation moved render target ranges, format, size, depth always written back after the draw shader module hash of SPH and code never, the key is the content

The rule: guest memory is the authority. Every GPU result is written back before submit returns, and a colour target whose pages changed outside its own draws is an error until loading is implemented, never a stale image. Remapping a VA to other pages changes what the next draw reads.

Why: identity by physical page survives remaps and aliasing, and nothing can show a frame the guest's memory does not hold. See ADR-0004.

docs.title: Deferred
docs.text:
item why it waits MME64 macros no Ampere header; the only public MME64 docs are Turing's syncpoint and channel ioctls, nvdrv, nvmap, address-space ioctls no loader or guest issues them yet semaphore acquire errors by name in the engine 2D, DMA and inline-to-memory classes not needed by the first scenes

Verified by: core/src/tests/gpu/fifo.rs and memory_map.rs, the engine acceptance test (draw, report, VA remap), and the QMD tests on its branch.

Sources: core/src/gpu/{fifo,threed,memory,engine}.rs, core/src/gpu/compute_class.rs on gpu/qmd-dispatch, NVIDIA's clc76f.h, clc797.h and clc7c0qmd.h.

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
The Switch 2's GPU runs the same SM86 machine code a desktop Ampere card runs, so CUDA kernels compiled with nvcc -arch=sm_86 are real guest-shaped programs. oboromi runs them two ways: through the translator on any Vulkan device, and natively on an NVIDIA card through libcuda.

flowchart LR
    CU["kernel.cu"] -->|"nvcc -arch=sm_86 -cubin"| CUBIN["cubin<br/>ELF64"]
    CUBIN --> LOAD["Kernel::load<br/>cubin.rs"]
    LOAD --> LAUNCH["Kernel::launch<br/>cbuf0 like the driver"]
    LAUNCH --> TR["translator + Vulkan<br/>any device"]
    SASS["SM86 program words"] --> WR["seed cubin writer<br/>cuda.rs"]
    WR --> NAT["libcuda.so.1<br/>NVIDIA card only"]
    TR --> CMP{"same bytes?"}
    NAT --> CMP

docs.title: The cubin runner
docs.text:
Kernel::load reads the ELF sections .text.<kernel>, .nv.info.<kernel>, .nv.constant<bank> and .nv.shared.<kernel>, takes the SM number from e_flags, accepts sm_80 to sm_89 only, and finds the parameter area from EIATTR_PARAM_CBANK and EIATTR_KPARAM_INFO. Kernel::launch fills constant bank 0 the way the CUDA driver does:

cbuf0 offset holds note 0x0 block dimensions ntid x, y, z 0xc grid dimensions nctaid x, y, z 0x28 initial stack pointer for R1 silicon gives a driver address; here the top of the translator's local array 0x118 memory descriptor zero on silicon, zero here 0x160 on kernel parameters offsets and sizes from KPARAM_INFO

Why this ABI: it was captured from the driver on silicon, so a cubin compiled today runs without patching.

docs.title: The native path
docs.text:
cuda.rs, behind the cuda feature, wraps a guest SM86 program in a cubin derived from a small seed kernel: it replaces .text, the parameter area, the shared size, the instruction offsets and the metadata, and keeps the seed's ELF header and segments. It opens libcuda.so.1 at run time with no new crate, then cuInit, context, cuModuleLoadData, cuLaunchKernel, synchronize. CudaDevice::run_native copies buffers in and out.

When it applies: a host with an NVIDIA card that loads sm_86 cubins and its driver, running compute programs. The translator stays the reference and the portable path; the native tests check both give the same bytes. Graphics stages do not go native.

docs.title: Kernels that run
docs.text:
kernel source result mul-add c[i] = a[i] * b[i] + i core/tests/fixtures/kernels.cu bit for bit equal to the RTX 3090 capture gradient core/tests/fixtures/kernels.cu same hash as on silicon Mandelbrot0, float NVIDIA cuda-samples, BSD-3 correct image, see below

measured, p50 per launch:

run device time Mandelbrot 800x600 on the translator Intel Arc (MTL) 10.2 ms gradient 1080p on the translator Intel Arc (MTL) 3.4 ms mul-add, native, copies included RTX A6000 1.0 ms gradient, native, copies included RTX A6000 6.8 ms Mandelbrot pixels equal to the sample's reference image 92.7 %

The Mandelbrot reference image's provenance is unknown, so that last row is a sanity check, not a pass mark.

Planned next, in order: nbody and particles, simpleTexture, Sobel, box and bilateral filters, fluids and smoke, marching cubes.

Verified by: cubin_kernels_match_silicon on Intel and lavapipe, and native_mul_add_matches_translator and native_gradient_matches_translator on the RTX A6000 (they skip without libcuda).

Sources: core/src/gpu/cubin.rs and core/src/gpu/cuda.rs on gpu-instructions, core/src/tests/gpu/cuda.rs, core/tests/fixtures/kernels.cu and cuda-seed.cu.

docs.title: Demos
docs.text: The window has three buttons that draw through the GPU work today, and four scenes are planned that each pull in the next missing feature. Every frame ends in display::present, which the Qt display widget shows.

docs.title: What runs today
docs.text:
button code what it proves Render Test Frame frame::render_test_frame a translated SASS program (S2R, IMAD, STG) writes a 1080p gradient through compute Demo frame::render_demo_frame a hand-assembled SASS Julia set animates every frame; time comes in through cbuf 0 Triangle frame::render_triangle_demo a pushbuffer in guest memory draws a turning triangle through the whole engine

The Julia set program uses FFMA, FMUL, FADD, FSETP, MUFU.COS, SIN and LG2, I2F, F2I, IADD3, IMAD, LOP3 and STG, with a predicated BRA loop. It re-dispatches one pipeline built once, so a frame costs a dispatch, a readback and a present.

measured on an Intel Arc (MTL), p50 per frame:

demo time test frame, 1080p 4.2 ms Julia set 4.7 ms pushbuffer triangle, 1080p 6.6 ms

docs.title: The planned scenes
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    TRI["triangle<br/>today"] --> PBR["pbr-boombox"]
    PBR --> POST["post-effect"]
    TRI --> SPR["sprites2d"]
    TRI --> PART["particles"]
    PBR -.->|"needs"| N1["indexed draws, depth,<br/>five textures, mips"]
    POST -.->|"needs"| N2["render to texture by VA,<br/>vertex-less draws"]
    PART -.->|"needs"| N3["QMD compute launch, instancing,<br/>blending"]
    SPR -.->|"needs"| N4["instancing, alpha blending,<br/>repeat-wrap sampling"]
scene content shaders pbr-boombox BoomBox or Avocado, metallic-roughness PBR with normal maps, one light pbr.vert, pbr.frag post-effect the PBR scene offscreen, then chromatic aberration, scanlines and a vignette post.vert, post.frag particles particles integrated by a compute dispatch, drawn as additive instanced quads particles_update.comp, particles.vert, particles.frag sprites2d parallax layers and floating sprites, alpha-blended over a procedural atlas sprite2d.vert, sprite2d.frag

Each scene document in demos/scenes lists its guest memory map, the register program it writes, and tags every unconfirmed convention with "(verify)". The shaders are GLSL that glslangValidator -V accepts; the plan is to compile them with the NVIDIA driver on a rented card into the SM86 programs the scenes load.

Why GLSL compiled on a desktop card: it gives real SM86 code for the stages, but not the Switch 2's shader header or attribute conventions, so those stay tagged until a real title shows them.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    GLB["glTF-Binary<br/>Khronos sample assets"] --> PY["scripts/gltf_to_raw.py"]
    PY --> V["vertices.bin<br/>position, normal, tangent, uv"]
    PY --> I["indices.bin<br/>u32"]
    PY --> T["slot.rgba8<br/>block-linear mip chain"]
    PY --> M["manifest.json<br/>layout, materials, source, licence"]

BoomBox and Avocado are CC0 1.0 by Microsoft, from KhronosGroup's glTF-Sample-Assets. Base colour and emissive are sRGB, the other slots linear. DamagedHelmet is avoided because its source carries a non-commercial licence.

docs.title: GPU pipeline
docs.text:
A guest asks the GPU for work by writing a pushbuffer into its own memory and pointing a GPFIFO entry at it. oboromi follows that path end to end: decode the methods, collect the 3D state into a snapshot at each draw, translate the guest's shader machine code, draw with Vulkan, and write the result back to guest memory, where the display reads it.

sequenceDiagram
    participant RAM as Guest RAM
    participant P as Pusher
    participant C as 3D class
    participant E as Engine
    participant T as Translator
    participant V as Vulkan
    E->>P: GPFIFO entries
    P->>RAM: fetch words
    P->>C: method writes
    C-->>P: DrawSnapshot
    P-->>E: events, in order
    E->>RAM: read SPH, SASS
    E->>T: SASS, stage
    T-->>E: SPIR-V
    E->>RAM: mirror buffers
    E->>V: pipeline, draw
    V-->>E: pixels
    E->>RAM: write back
    Note over E,RAM: present reads the surface from guest RAM

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
step code output decode GPFIFO entry and method headers fifo.rs Pusher::submit method writes per subchannel bind classes with SET_OBJECT, run channel methods fifo.rs channel semaphore events keep the 3D register file, snapshot at draw triggers threed.rs ThreeD::write Event::Draw(DrawSnapshot) read shader headers and code, translate engine.rs module, sm86 translate_program SPIR-V, cached by SPH and code hash mirror buffers the draw reads engine.rs mirror host buffers keyed by guest-physical ranges draw and read back graphics.rs VkState::draw RGBA8 pixels write back and present engine.rs draw, present guest memory, then display::present

Why synchronous: Gpu::submit returns only after every draw has landed in guest memory, so any later CPU read sees it. See ADR-0006.

Why a snapshot: the draw sees the registers as they were at the trigger, and later method writes cannot change a draw in flight.

Compute work takes the same road through class 0xC7C0: a QMD in guest memory becomes a dispatch snapshot (see command processor). Its execution in the engine is not wired yet.

docs.title: oboromi overview
docs.text:
oboromi is a Rust emulator for the Nintendo Switch 2, with a Qt front end over a C FFI. It is early: it cannot boot firmware or a game. This page maps the parts outside the GPU in rough strokes, so the GPU pages have context.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Front["front end"]
        QT["Qt window<br/>buttons, display widget"] --> BR["RustBridge.cpp"]
    end
    BR -->|"extern C"| FFI["core/src/ffi.rs"]
    FFI --> TESTS["tests<br/>CPU and GPU self-tests"]
    FFI --> GPU["gpu<br/>frames and demos"]
    subgraph Core["oboromi-core"]
        SYS["sys::State<br/>one field per service"]
        NN["nn<br/>service stubs, HIPC header"]
        CPU["cpu::CpuManager<br/>8 Unicorn AArch64 cores"]
        RAM[("guest RAM<br/>flat, base 0")]
        FS["fs<br/>memory-mapped files"]
        AUD["audio<br/>empty"]
    end
    SYS --> NN
    CPU --> RAM
    TESTS --> CPU

docs.title: The parts
docs.text: part where what it does today state CPU cores core/src/cpu eight Unicorn AArch64 cores share one pinned RAM block; run, step, registers, reads and writes real guest RAM cpu_manager.rs one flat 12 GiB block at address 0, lazily backed by the host OS real loader none no NSO, NRO or ELF loader, so guest code is placed by tests missing SVCs and hooks none no supervisor calls, no memory hooks missing services core/src/nn a State {} per service name, registered by start_host_services; HIPC decodes a header and ignores it stub GPU services nn: nvdrv, nvmap names, vi, host1x names only, no ioctls; the GPU work drives the GPU directly stub filesystem core/src/fs a memory-mapped file wrapper stub audio core/src/audio empty module stub display core/src/display.rs holds the last presented RGBA8 frame and calls the GUI back real FFI core/src/ffi.rs test runners, frame render calls, frame read and callback real GUI gui-qt CPU and GPU test buttons, Render Test Frame, Demo and Triangle toggles, the display widget real

docs.title: How a frame reaches the window
docs.text:
The core never touches the GUI. A renderer calls display::present, which bumps a generation counter, copies the pixels and fires the registered C callback. The Qt display widget then reads the frame through FFI and letterboxes it.

Why: event driven, no polling, and the core stays testable without a window.

docs.title: What this means for the GPU work
docs.text:
Nothing upstream of the GPU exists yet: no game issues ioctls, and no channel or address space is set up by the OS layer. So the GPU work starts at the hardware interface and is driven by host-written pushbuffers in guest memory. When a loader and nvdrv exist, they plug in where those tests write today.

Verified by: the CPU self-tests (core/src/tests/run.rs, multicore_test.rs) and an offscreen screenshot of the window after Render Test Frame.

docs.title: Honest limits
docs.text:
• No game boots. There is no loader, and the GPU is driven by host-written pushbuffers.
  • Nothing has run on a Switch 2. Instruction semantics are verified on GA102 (RTX 3090, A6000), which is the same Ampere SM; the T239's encoding table is identical, its runtime behaviour is assumed equal by design.
  • Shader program header size: the engine reads code after a 0x50-byte header and finds its end at the branch-to-self; NAK says the version 4 header is 32 words, which puts code at 0x80. Unresolved until a real title's shader is read.
  • The GPU page size is Ryujinx's big page size; the T239 value is unverified.
  • The base-vertex behaviour of VertexIndex and the front-facing value are unverified.
  • Graphics-stage code has only been written by hand and by desktop compilers, never taken from a Switch 2 title.

Verified by: each "done" row links to its tests on the subsystem page; "in progress" rows are unmerged branches.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/*.rs (named todos), core/src/gpu/engine.rs (errors by name), core/src/gpu/memory.rs, demos/README, PR #79 and #80.

docs.title: SASS translator
docs.text: The translator turns SM86 machine code into one SPIR-V module per program. It decodes each 128-bit instruction with a table generated from NVIDIA's own instruction description, keeps the guest register file in shader memory, and runs the program as a loop over a program counter.

docs.title: Decoder
docs.text:
scripts/decoder_generator.rs reads scripts/sm_86_instructions.txt, the instruction table nvdisasm carries (extracted the DocumentSASS way), and writes sm86_decoder_generated.rs: one branch per encoding class, keyed on bit 91 and bits 11:0, calling a handler per opcode family. Alternate-syntax classes are skipped so a pseudo-op never shadows the real instruction. An unknown word panics.

Why the SM86 table for the Switch 2's T239: CUDA 13.1's nvdisasm ships byte-identical tables for SM86, SM87 and SM88, and SM88 is the T239's GA10F. No class, field or key differs. See ADR-0007.

docs.title: State model
docs.text: guest state SPIR-V home note R0 to R253, RZ Private u32 array per invocation RZ reads zero P0 to P6, PT one Private word of bits PT is constant true UR0 to UR62, UP same array, after the predicates uniform datapath live last word of the array dead lanes start past the end pc, return pcs, BSSY tokens B0 to B15 Private variables local memory Private array 4 KiB per lane shared memory Workgroup array 1 KiB per workgroup warp exchange, schedule slots Workgroup arrays collectives and divergence

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    start["pc = 0"] --> loop{"pc < program length?"}
    loop -->|"no"| done["return"]
    loop -->|"yes"| sw["switch on pc<br/>one case per basic block"]
    sw --> blk["block: guarded instructions,<br/>a branch stores the next pc"]
    blk --> loop

Vulkan only takes structured control flow, so guest branches store a pc and one loop around a switch dispatches on it. Basic blocks start at 0, at branch targets, after branches and EXIT, at BSYNC and after BAR. A program with BRX, JMX or CALL through a register makes every pc a leader. EXIT stores a pc past the end. A predicated instruction @Pg is wrapped in a selection on its predicate; uniform ops guard on UP.

docs.title: Divergence
docs.text:
A warp is 32 consecutive invocations. Programs without collectives keep a free per-lane loop. Programs with VOTE, SHFL, MATCH, REDUX, BAR, tensor ops, LDSM, MOVM or R2UR.OR run workgroup-uniform: each step every invocation votes, the lowest runnable pc runs, lanes at other pcs sit the step out with their effects masked. Collectives trade values through a Workgroup array between two barriers. BSSY stores a token per lane; BSYNC blocks while a warp peer holds the same token elsewhere. BAR arrivals are counted per barrier id and released when complete. A stuck program reports live = 2 and the harness panics.

Why: workgroup barriers must be reached by every invocation, and lavapipe's subgroups are 8 wide, so native subgroups cannot carry a 32-lane warp everywhere. See ADR-0003.

docs.title: Set-0 binding ABI and stages
docs.text:
binding kind holds 0 uniform buffer host support data, never a guest cbuf 1 to 8 uniform buffers guest cbuf slots 0 to 7, std140 uvec4 arrays 9 storage buffer the global memory window 10, 11 storage buffers register in and out, tests only 12 on image samplers, storage images textures and surfaces, dense in first-use order

Stages: Stage::Compute { local_size }, Vertex, Fragment { flat, screen_linear, depth }. ALD and AST are vertex-only, IPA fragment-only. Attribute space: position at 0x70, generic n at 0x80 + 16n, instance id 0x2f8, vertex id 0x2fc, front facing 0x3fc. Interpolation comes from the pixel SPH, not from IPA.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
measure count encoding classes decoded 999 handler functions 176 handlers left as named todos 19 named sub-form todos inside implemented handlers 13

By design todo: graphics-only transport (ISBERD, ISBEWR, LDTRAM, OUT, PIXLD), ray tracing (six TTU ops), sparse tensor (GATHER, SCATTER, GENMETADATA, SPMETADATA, BITEXTRACT), FOOTPRINT, SUQUERY, UCLEA, float atomics, ATOM ARRIVE, CAST and SAFEADD, BAR.SCAN, implicit-LOD TEX in compute. docs.title: Textures and tensors
docs.text: Two families need more than a one-line lowering. Textures need the guest's descriptor pools decoded into Vulkan images and samplers. Tensor core ops need the exact way Ampere adds up products, which no Vulkan float operation reproduces.

docs.title: Textures
docs.text:
A texture handle is a word in a constant buffer: the low 20 bits index the TIC pool (texture headers), the top 12 bits index the TSC pool (samplers). The translator records where each handle comes from, (cbuf bank, byte offset), and gives each distinct one a set-0 binding from 12. The host reads the handle, decodes both pool entries and binds an image with its sampler.

flowchart LR
    CB["cbuf word<br/>handle"] --> TIC["TIC entry<br/>format, size, layout, levels"]
    CB --> TSC["TSC entry<br/>wrap, filters, LOD"]
    TIC --> DET{"layout"}
    DET -->|"pitch"| PL["rows as they are<br/>one level"]
    DET -->|"block-linear"| BL["deswizzle GOBs<br/>per mip level"]
    PL --> IMG["HostImage"]
    BL --> IMG
    TSC --> SMP["VkSampler"]
    IMG --> BIND["binding 12 on"]
    SMP --> BIND
decoded supported layouts pitch-linear with one level, block-linear with a mip chain formats A8B8G8R8 UNORM and sRGB, R8, G8R8, R16G16B16A16 float, R32 UINT, BC1, BC3, BC7 type and swizzle 2D, identity swizzle sampler repeat or clamp to edge, nearest or linear, mip filter and LOD clamp rejected by name other formats, swizzles and types, depth compare, anisotropy, reduction filters, unnormalized TSC

Block-linear: a GOB is 64 bytes by 8 rows with 16-byte sectors interleaved, GOBs stack into blocks along Y, and the block height shrinks per mip level as Ryujinx's size calculator does.

On the translator side: TEX, TLD, TLD4, TXD, TXQ and TMML sample through combined image samplers; SULD, SUST, SURED and SUATOM use storage images. TMML gets its derivatives from compute-shader derivative groups.

Why provenance, not handle values: the handle's source is known at translation time and its value is not. Unknown provenance fails by name.

docs.title: Tensor cores
docs.text:
HMMA, IMMA, DMMA, BMMA, LDSM and MOVM run per lane: lane 4g + t holds row g of a fragment, and each source register is shared through one warp exchange.

Silicon does not sum HMMA products in IEEE order. The model reproduced bit for bit:

step rule grouping products in groups of 8 k (4 for TF32), C joins the group sum alignment every term aligned to the largest exponent; a product's exponent is ea + eb truncation bits below 2^(emax-24) are dropped, not rounded sum exact integer sum, normalised to f32 by truncation .F16 result each group rounds to f16 inf and NaN an IEEE sum of only the special terms

Why loops: written straight out, the exact model is a huge module that drivers take long to compile. A SPIR-V function was inlined back by both drivers. So operands are staged once in a Private array and the sum runs in four DontUnroll loops. See ADR-0005.

per HMMA.16816.F32, cold pipeline compile:

form SPIR-V words Intel lavapipe IEEE order, unrolled 3.1k 18 ms 0.8 s exact model, unrolled 15.8k 0.6 to 1 s 2.5 s exact model, one function 3.1k 940 ms 6.0 s exact model, DontUnroll loops 4.9k 57 ms 0.2 s

Verified by: the tensor silicon scoreboard (session 5 captures) passing on Intel and lavapipe, texture and surface captures from CUDA texture objects, and the block-linear swizzle checked against the Python asset converter.

Sources: core/src/gpu/texture.rs, core/src/gpu/sm86/{texture,tensor}.rs, core/src/tests/gpu/{texture,tensor}.rs.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Every claim about the GPU work rests on one of four tiers, cheapest first. A handler is not done until it passes the tiers that apply to it, on Intel and on lavapipe.

flowchart TB
    T1["1. spirv-val<br/>every emitted module is valid SPIR-V"] --> T2["2. nvdisasm<br/>every hand-built word is the instruction we think"]
    T2 --> T3["3. silicon captures<br/>results match an RTX 3090 / A6000"]
    T3 --> T4["4. compiled programs<br/>nvcc kernels and CUDA samples end to end"]
tier how where spirv-val the harness pipes each module through spirv-val, skipped when it is not installed core/src/tests/gpu/harness.rs nvdisasm fixtures_match_nvdisasm disassembles the test words and compares the text core/src/tests/gpu_test.rs silicon scoreboard tests replay captured inputs and compare registers, shared, global and image bytes core/src/tests/gpu/fixtures.rs, core/tests/fixtures programs nvcc-built kernels run through the translator and match silicon output or its hash core/src/tests/gpu/program.rs, cubin tests

docs.title: How silicon captures are made
docs.text:
Each capture patches one 128-bit instruction word into an nvcc-compiled seed kernel, launches it through the CUDA driver API on a rented RTX 3090 or A6000, and reads the registers and memory back. Words are built from the instruction table and checked with nvdisasm before launch. A fixture records the word, inputs, outputs and whether it was really observed; observed results are never hand-written.

session device what it added 1 RTX 3090 single-instruction integer cases warp RTX A6000 votes, shuffles, reductions, shared memory, barriers 3 RTX 3090 fp32, fp16, fp64, conversions, predicates, warp, textures 4 RTX 3090 whole programs, DSETP, HSETP2, atomics, textures 5 RTX 3090 observers, local memory, TMML, SUATOM, tensors, driver cbuf0 values fixture file captures sm86-thread.jsonl 136 sm86-predicate.jsonl 209 sm86-warp.jsonl 220 sm86-texture.jsonl 37 sm86-observer.jsonl 31 sm86-tensor.jsonl 15

Known failures are named per fixture id and per device, each with its reason: KNOWN_FAILURES hold everywhere (MUFU.TANH is a hardware approximation, SUATOM lane order is up to the device), LLVMPIPE_FAILURES only on lavapipe (f64 RoundEven truncates, an infinite unnormalized coordinate reads texel 0). See ADR-0008.

docs.title: What each tier caught
docs.text:
bug caught by EXIT emitted OpKill, which compute shaders may not use spirv-val vector types read type id 0, OpMemberName in the wrong section spirv-val MOV immediate keyed on 0x1a02, which is really MOV from cx[UR]; the real key is 0x802 nvdisasm test words carried guard P0 instead of PT nvdisasm drivers folded x + -x to zero, Intel flushed f16 and f64 denormals fp32 tests, then silicon fp16 and fp64 cases NaN results: fp32 and fp16 are canonical, fp64 keeps the first NaN's payload silicon HMMA summed in IEEE order instead of the truncating group sum silicon tensor captures SHFL with a clamp of 15 was read as a half-warp segment; it clamps the whole warp silicon, a later session LDG/STG with a memory descriptor added the descriptor to the address compiled program (nvcc mul-add) I2F to f32 ignored directed rounding CUDA sample (Mandelbrot) IADD3 ignored the negate bit on cbuf and uniform operands CUDA sample (Mandelbrot) IMAD.HI added Rc as 32 bits instead of the 64-bit pair CUDA sample (Mandelbrot) narrow stores raced as a plain read-modify-write review; now a compare-exchange loop HFMA2 rounded twice through native f16 fma on lavapipe review; now one rounding from a round-to-odd f32 sum BAR.RED wrote its result to Rb instead of B2R.RESULT divergence work

The lesson in the last group: whole compiled programs find bugs the per-instruction captures miss, in operand flags, rounding modes and register pairs.

docs.title: Perf and CI
docs.text:
core/examples/perf.rs prints p50, p95, p99 and max for translate, dispatch, draw, the demo frames and the pushbuffer triangle. scripts/profile.sh records it with perf and writes a report and a flamegraph. CI builds and tests on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS; only Ubuntu has a Vulkan device (lavapipe), the others skip the GPU tests. Ubuntu also prints the perf baseline.

Verified by: this page is the index of checks; each tier's tests are listed above.

Sources: core/src/tests/gpu/{harness,fixtures,program}.rs, core/src/tests/gpu_test.rs, core/tests/fixtures/README, core/examples/perf.rs, scripts/profile.sh, .github/workflows/ci.yml.

docs.title: Vulkan backend
docs.text:
The backend owns one Vulkan device and runs everything synchronously on one queue: compute dispatches for translated compute programs and CUDA kernels, graphics draws for the engine. Every submit waits on a fence and reads results back to host memory before it returns.

flowchart TB
    DEV["gpu::device()<br/>VkState, created once"] --> Q["one GRAPHICS and COMPUTE queue<br/>one command pool"]
    Q --> SUB["Submit<br/>one command buffer + one fence, behind a Mutex"]
    SUB --> CP["ComputePipeline<br/>dispatch"]
    SUB --> GP["GraphicsPipeline<br/>draw with dynamic rendering"]
    CP --> D0["Descriptors<br/>set 0"]
    GP --> D0
    D0 --> HB["HostBuffer<br/>cbufs, global window, vertices"]
    D0 --> HI["HostImage<br/>textures and surfaces"]
    GP --> RT["RenderTarget<br/>RGBA8 + optional D32"]

docs.title: Parts
docs.text: part file role VkState gpu/mod.rs instance, physical device, device, queue, pool, feature flags HostBuffer gpu/compute.rs host-visible buffer, cached memory preferred, explicit flush and invalidate HostImage gpu/compute.rs 2D image uploaded through staging with all its mip levels, kept in GENERAL Descriptors gpu/compute.rs the set-0 layout shared by compute and graphics ComputePipeline gpu/compute.rs compute pipeline; VkState::dispatch records, barriers, submits, waits GraphicsPipeline gpu/graphics.rs vertex + fragment pipeline for one colour format and optional depth RenderTarget gpu/graphics.rs offscreen colour and depth images, read back after each draw

docs.title: Device choices
docs.text:
choice why Vulkan 1.3, first device with a GRAPHICS and COMPUTE queue dynamic rendering without render pass objects shaderFloat16, shaderFloat64, shaderInt64 when present fp16, fp64 and 64-bit integer SASS ops int64 buffer and shared atomics when present 64-bit ATOM and ATOMS; Intel lacks the shared one VK_KHR_compute_shader_derivatives, linear groups TMML and derivatives in compute programs SignedZeroInfNanPreserve and DenormPreserve per width drivers fold x + -x to zero and Intel flushes f16 and f64 denormals; the guest does neither a missing ICD maps to NoDevice tests skip cleanly on machines without Vulkan

Dynamic state, so one pipeline serves every value: viewport, scissor, cull mode, front face, primitive topology within its class, depth test, depth write, depth compare and blend constants. The pipeline key keeps only what Vulkan cannot change at draw time: shader hashes, vertex layout, topology class, colour write mask and the depth attachment.

docs.title: Latency rules
docs.text:
• No allocation per frame: the device is a process-wide singleton, the command buffer and fence are reused, demo pipelines are built once and kept in a static.
  • Cached host memory for readback, since reads from uncached memory are slow.
  • The engine caches modules by SPH and code hash, pipelines by key, buffer mirrors by guest-physical ranges, and refreshes a mirror only when its pages changed.

measured on an Intel Arc (MTL), p50, cargo run --release -p oboromi-core --example perf:

path latency translate 1000 instructions 326 µs dispatch, fence and readback 135 µs draw and readback, 64x64 triangle 193 µs 1080p test frame end to end 4.2 ms Julia demo frame end to end 4.7 ms pushbuffer triangle at 1080p 6.6 ms

docs.title: lavapipe as the CI device
docs.text:
The Ubuntu CI job installs mesa's lavapipe and spirv-tools, pins VK_DRIVER_FILES to the lavapipe ICD, runs the whole suite on it and then runs the perf example as a latency baseline. Every GPU test also runs locally on Intel. Where lavapipe differs from silicon, the fixture lists say so per device.

Verified by: the Vulkan validation layer clean on Intel and lavapipe for dispatch, draw and depth paths; the suite skipping without an ICD.

Sources: core/src/gpu/{mod,compute,graphics,engine}.rs, core/examples/perf.rs, .github/workflows/ci.yml, PR #79 body.
